label: Gambling and the Bet
framing: Scripture never names the lottery, but it names the heart that wants wealth without work and money it has not earned. The bet promises that one night can undo a hard life, and that promise is the lie that empties the table.
cultural: Casting lots was common in the ancient world, used to divide land, choose duties, and even pick an apostle, but always as a way of submitting a decision to God, never as a wager against a neighbor. The soldiers gambling for the robe of Jesus at the foot of the cross are Scripture's sharpest picture of the bet, men playing for a stranger's last possession while the world's deepest loss unfolds above their heads.
historical: The early church and the Reformers alike warned against games of chance, seeing in them both the love of money and the wish to gain from another's loss. John Wesley, in the eighteenth century, told his societies to gain all they can by honest labor, drawing a hard line between earning and merely winning, and the church has long read the desire to get rich quick as a snare rather than a gift.
application: Be honest about what the bet is actually for, which is rarely money and usually escape. Set a hard wall between yourself and the trigger, the app, the account, the route past the machines. And if you have tried to stop and cannot, this is no longer a habit but an addiction, and addiction is not beaten by willpower alone but by help. In the United States you can reach free, confidential help any hour at SAMHSA, 1-800-662-4357.

verses.text: A faithful man will abound with blessings, but one eager to be rich will not go unpunished. A stingy man hastens after wealth and does not know that poverty awaits him.
verses.where: Within three verses Proverbs warns twice about the hurry to be rich: the one eager to be rich will not go unpunished, and the one who hastens after wealth does not see the poverty waiting for him. The site's note says the chapter commends integrity over wealth and warns against greed. The hurry itself is the danger these proverbs name.

verses.text: He who loves money is never satisfied by money, and he who loves wealth is never satisfied by income. This too is futile.
verses.where: The Teacher says that the one who loves money is never satisfied by money, and the one who loves wealth is never satisfied by income. The site's note on the chapter says he shows how the love of money never satisfies, and how riches can be hoarded or lost. A win does not end the wanting; it feeds it.

verses.text: Those who want to be rich, however, fall into temptation and become ensnared by many foolish and harmful desires that plunge them into ruin and destruction. For the love of money is the root of all kinds of evil. By craving it, some have wandered away from the faith and pierced themselves with many sorrows.
verses.where: Paul warns that those who want to be rich fall into a trap of foolish and harmful desires, and that by craving money some have wandered from the faith and pierced themselves with many sorrows. The site's plain note sets beside it Paul's own picture, godliness with contentment as great gain, and asks whether you want to be rich and what that wanting is doing to you.

verses.text: Keep your lives free from the love of money and be content with what you have, for God has said: “Never will I leave you, never will I forsake you.”
verses.where: Among the letter's closing instructions is this one: keep your life free from the love of money and be content with what you have, because God has said he will never leave or forsake you. The site's plain note says the verse is not a promise that God will make anyone rich, nor a rebuke of people who are poor, but a call to be free from the love of money, whatever you have.

verses.text: “Everything is permissible for me,” but not everything is beneficial. “Everything is permissible for me,” but I will not be mastered by anything.
verses.where: Some in Corinth lived by a slogan, everything is permissible for me, and Paul answers it with two questions: is it beneficial, and is it mastering me. The site's plain note says the slogan is still one people live by. A thing can be allowed and still be in charge.

verses.text: He who conceals his sins will not prosper, but whoever confesses and renounces them will find mercy.
verses.where: The site's note calls this one of the Bible's clearest sayings on confession: the one who conceals his sins will not prosper, but the one who confesses and renounces them will find mercy. Its note on the word for conceal says the same verb is used of God covering sin in forgiveness, and that the difference is who does the covering. A habit that lives on secrecy begins to lose its hold when it is told.

verses.text: Finally he came to his senses and said, ‘How many of my father’s hired servants have plenty of food? But here I am, starving to death! I will get up and go back to my father and say to him, “Father, I have sinned against heaven and against you. I am no longer worthy to be called your son. Make me like one of your hired servants.”’ So he got up and went to his father. But while he was still in the distance, his father saw him and was filled with compassion. He ran to his son, embraced him, and kissed him.
verses.where: The younger son has squandered his share of the estate in a far country, and when he is starving he comes to his senses and starts for home, rehearsing a speech about working as a hired servant. The site's note says his father sees him far off and runs to him before the son says a word. The plain note says the turning matters, and the welcome is a gift.

verses.text: The lot is cast into the lap, but its every decision is from the LORD.
verses.where: In Israel lots were cast to settle a question, and Proverbs says that every decision of the lot is from the LORD. The site's note on the word says the point is that even this apparently random act lies under God's rule. When Scripture describes casting lots, it is usually a way of leaving a decision to God, not a wager.

verses.text: When the soldiers had crucified Jesus, they divided His garments into four parts, one for each soldier, with the tunic remaining. It was seamless, woven in one piece from top to bottom. So they said to one another, “Let us not tear it. Instead, let us cast lots to see who will get it.” This was to fulfill the Scripture: “They divided My garments among them, and cast lots for My clothing.” So that is what the soldiers did.
verses.where: At the foot of the cross, four soldiers divide Jesus' clothes and cast lots for his seamless tunic. The site's note says John sees even the soldiers' gambling as the fulfillment of Scripture, the psalm of the righteous sufferer enacted in its details. They played for a dying man's last possession while he gave his life above them.

verses.text: Brothers, if someone is caught in a trespass, you who are spiritual should restore him with a spirit of gentleness. But watch yourself, or you also may be tempted. Carry one another’s burdens, and in this way you will fulfill the law of Christ.
verses.where: Paul tells the church that when someone is caught in a trespass, those who are spiritual should restore him gently, watching themselves, and that believers should carry one another's burdens. The site's plain note says restoring a person is a beautiful thing churches should practise, and that gentleness toward the one who fell never means keeping serious wrongs quiet. For a family facing someone's gambling, both halves hold: gentleness, and the truth.

related.label: When You Are Trapped by Addiction

links.label: Addiction and the Long Road Back
Practical guides for work and money

whole: If gambling has left you in debt you cannot see your way out of, or you have had thoughts of hurting yourself, tell someone you trust today; the Find Help page on this site lists places to turn. For most people who search for this, the question is not whether a raffle ticket is a sin. It is the app opened again at two in the morning, the rent money that went on one more bet, the losses hidden from a husband or a wife, the borrowing to win it back. Or it is the person on the other side, a parent, a spouse or a child who has found the statements and no longer knows what is true.

Scripture never names the lottery or the casino, but it names what drives them. Proverbs warns against the hurry to be rich. The Teacher of Ecclesiastes says the one who loves money is never satisfied by money, which is the whole logic of chasing a loss. Paul says those who want to be rich fall into a trap of desires that plunge them into ruin, and he asks of any habit whether it is mastering you. Proverbs names the secrecy too: the one who conceals his sins will not prosper. Underneath, the bet usually promises more than money. It promises that one night can undo a hard life, or it offers a few hours away from what hurts.

So the first wisdom is honesty. Tell the truth to God and to the person your losses have touched, because what is hidden keeps its hold, and Proverbs promises mercy to the one who confesses and renounces. Ask Paul's two questions, whether it is good for you and whether it is mastering you, and answer them by what you do rather than what you intend: if you chase losses, hide them, borrow to play, or cannot stop when you try, it has become a grip, and a grip needs help, not willpower alone. Put walls between yourself and the trigger: the app, the account, the route past the machines. Get sound advice about the debts early. And if you love someone caught in this, restore gently, as Paul says, without covering for it or carrying alone what was never yours to carry.

The hope here is a Father, not a jackpot. In Jesus' story the son who wasted everything came to his senses and started home, rehearsing a speech about working as a hired servant, and his father ran to him before he could finish it. Hebrews tells people tempted by money to be content with what they have, because God has said he will never leave them or forsake them. Contentment is not a smaller life. It is a life no longer waiting on the next turn of a card.

differ.share: Christians agree that Scripture never names gambling, that the love of money is the root of all kinds of evil, and that some lines are hard: betting money your household needs is wrong (1 Timothy 5:8), and chasing losses, hiding them, or borrowing to play are signs of a grip that needs help, not a debate.

views.name: Wrong in itself
views.body: Some hold that gambling is wrong in itself. It feeds the wish to get rich, which 1 Timothy 6:9 warns can plunge people into ruin; it seeks gain from a neighbor's loss rather than from work (Ephesians 4:28); and they want no part in an industry that profits from people who cannot stop.

views.name: A small stake as entertainment
views.body: Others hold that a small bet among friends, a raffle, or a lottery ticket bought for fun is spending on entertainment, no different in principle from a ticket to a game, and that making a rule of it goes beyond Scripture (Colossians 2:20-23). Kept small, they say, it is a freedom to enjoy with thanks.

differ.after: No creed settles this, and faithful churches answer it differently. The site's Find Help page on drinking, tattoos and gambling sets out both views and does not choose, and neither does this page. Where a grip has formed, the question is no longer whether it is allowed.

deep.sit: What is the bet really for, the money or a few hours away from something else, and who is the one person you need to tell the truth to first?

prayer.lead: The site's plain note says this psalm does not shame you; it tells you what silence costs and what confession gives. Notice how quickly God forgives in verse 5.
prayer.text: When I kept silent, my bones became brittle from my groaning all day long. For day and night Your hand was heavy upon me; my strength was drained as in the summer heat. Selah Then I acknowledged my sin to You and did not hide my iniquity. I said, “I will confess my transgressions to the LORD,” and You forgave the guilt of my sin.

careLines.text: If you are worn down by failing again and again, or caught in an addiction you cannot break, you are not alone, and you are not beyond help.
Please talk to someone: a doctor, a pastor, a counsellor, or a group that helps people with what you are facing.
If you are in money trouble now, look for a trusted adviser where you live; these notes are not financial advice.
The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
